articles.title: Libghostty 1.0
articles.content: libghostty-vt 1.0 is here. libghostty is a portable, high-performance C library for terminal emulation, extracted directly from the core of Ghostty. The 1.0 release means both the library itself and the C ABI are now stable. A little over a year ago, I wrote that libghostty is coming . At the time, the Zig module had just been merged, the C API didn't exist, and nobody but Ghostty was a consumer. Today, the C API is a complete terminal emulator, it runs in production for millions of people across hundreds of products, both free and commercial, and it has a real, enforced ABI stability policy. This post is about how we got here and what 1.0 actually means. 1 Who Is Already Using It Since starting the Ghostty project in 2022, the most common question I've been asked is "why?". I already answered this in the libghostty is coming post, so feel free to read that if you wish. Today, I'd rather answer this by showing the broad industry impact libghostty has already had . I believe this strongly validates its existence. A year ago, I used a bug in JediTerm , the terminal emulator in JetBrains IDEs, as an example of why terminal emulation is hard to get right. A year later, the terminal in JetBrains IDEs now runs on libghostty . Every IntelliJ, PyCharm, GoLand, etc. user now has a libghostty-powered terminal. Based on a report by JetBrains, that's over 12.5 million active users. Neovim has an approved pull request replacing libvterm with libghostty-vt . Among other things, it closes a 10-year-old issue about reflowing scrollback on resize. The maintainers are waiting on a tagged release before merging so that distributions can package the dependency separately, and the release today should enable that. KDE developers are experimenting with a Konsole replacement built on it. Vercel's Turborepo uses it to render task output in its TUI. devenv uses it to drive shells. Antithesis used it to fuzz TUI programs and found real bugs in btop and others. Ghostel brings it to Emacs. ghostty-web is the WASM build with an Xterm.js-compatible API. Commercial products like OrbStack embed it. And a whole wave of new terminals and "agentic" coding tools, such as herdr and cmux , have been built on it rather than writing yet another emulator. There are community bindings for Rust, Go, JavaScript, Swift, Python, .NET, Elixir, Dart, Java, and more, and the awesome-libghostty list tracks well over a hundred projects. More people today use a terminal powered by libghostty than use Ghostty the application, by a very large multiple. And libghostty is having a much larger impact than being "just" a terminal emulator. 2 ABI Stability 1.0 means libghostty-vt follows semantic versioning and has strict ABI compatibility promises so that packagers across distributions and operating systems can be confident packaging libghostty-vt and program developers can be confident dynamically linking against it. Beyond providing useful features, I believe the hallmark of a high-quality and endurin
articles.summary: Ghostty 团队发布 libghostty-vt 1.0，这是从 Ghostty 核心提取的高性能终端模拟 C 库，库本身与 C ABI 均已稳定。

articles.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production
articles.content: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks that ultimately only sold in just a handful of markets because of its heavy, angular design. Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla's robotaxi ambitions. While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model's specialized components. In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era." Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours. The US EV maker only began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Before the pickup truck launched, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units. "It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same." "It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves." Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Its angular design was mocked by pickup truck purists and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe. The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them - only to leave massive cracks in two of them. During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future." But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations. Automotive analyst Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pick-ups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market. "All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren't popular in the US," Munoz said. But Cybertruck's sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact. "Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said. articles.title: A Jev that can ask Opus for help gives Opus accuracy at 4x lower cost
articles.content: We wanted to test whether LLMs and decision models, specifically Jev and Luna, could solve a hard problem that we encounter regularly (grading identity resolution results). We found that while both models performed okay out of the box (88.8–97.3% accuracy), implementing a hybrid model that combines Jev + Opus achieves frontier accuracy at > 4x lower costs. Our other findings: Luna performs better than Jev out of the box, but the gap disappears on harder cases. Jev's confidence is better calibrated. Most of its mistakes come with low confidence its right. Most of Luna's mistakes come with high confidence. This enables Jev to perform better than Luna in a hybrid model harness. Frontier models are still more accurate than decision models Decision models are up to 90× cheaper and more than 10× faster out of the box. They cost $0.05 - $0.10 per 1,000 identities and answer in about 0.15 seconds, but trail Opus accuracy by about 6 percentage points on harder benchmarks. What is identity resolution? Identity resolution is the process of mapping data to corresponding real people. More precisely, say you have a set of data records D . Determine a set of identities I and mapping m(D)->I such that each record d ∈ D maps to an identity i ∈ I , each i corresponds to exactly one real person in the real world, and no two i correspond to the same person in the real world. This is foundational for any company wishing to do outreach, personalization, or analytics on customers. You can’t know, for instance, the lifetime value of a customer without being able to map all their purchases to a single identity. For example, the input data might contain the following records. IDR would ideally create one identity, Alice , and associate all of these records with Alice . Name Email Home address Shipping address loyalty_record_1 Alice alice@alice.com — — loyalty_record_2 Alice — 123 Main St — transaction_record_1 Alice — — 123 Main St transaction_record_2 (null) alice@alice.com — Store Pickup In practice, IDR is very difficult. People share emails, move addresses, etc. There might also be errors in the data. See some examples here: Error Type What it looks like What it could also mean Typo Valentino → Valentinp A different surname Misread character Sam → 5am Garbage, or a username Spelled how it sounds Phillips → Filips A different family Month and day swapped 02/17/2020 → 17/02/2020 A birth date that doesn’t parse Value copied from a relative A child listed with a parent’s birth date An adult with the child’s name Nickname Robert → Bob Two brothers Placeholder name Valentino → Female Child Nothing useful at all Blank field Mendoza → (blank) Anyone The most common and problematic issue with IDR is over-merging . This is when an identity i incorrectly corresponds to multiple people in the real world. articles.title: Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2
articles.content: Firecracker is supposed to keep untrusted code inside a microVM. We escaped it and achieved code execution as root on the host. We found how it saved registers, changed where it would resume, and made it execute a call of our choosing when it returned from KVM. The guest then restored the temporary stack changes. Firecracker kept running, and the VM remained accessible over SSH. PwnEscape Part 1 introduced the host memory primitive behind this work. Here we follow the next part of the chain: using that access to find Firecracker in memory and take over a live thread from inside the guest. This is a continuation to show CVE-2026-99999 on a Firecracker setup. 00 / Choosing where to take control A Firecracker microVM has a process on the host that manages it. Each virtual CPU, or vCPU, has a thread in that process. The thread enters KVM to run the guest and returns to Firecracker when an event needs handling in userspace. Firecracker documents this arrangement in its architecture overview . firecracker-host-integration-dbdde36ef234 The call that runs the virtual CPU looks like this: ioctl(vcpu_fd, KVM_RUN, 0 ); While the thread is in that system call, the host kernel holds its saved userspace registers in a structure called pt_regs . These registers describe the Firecracker thread: its instruction pointer says where execution should resume, and its stack pointer says which userspace stack it should use. That made the return from KVM_RUN an attractive target. If we could locate and modify the saved frame, we could choose the code Firecracker executed when the thread returned to userspace. A guest operation that caused such a return would provide the trigger. We already had access to selected host physical memory through a guest mapping. To use it, we needed to identify the Firecracker process, find code we could call in that process, and locate the register frame belonging to its active vCPU thread. The starting point was a page of memory we controlled inside the guest. 01-guest-to-vmm-chain-5c0fbee0cb07 Figure 1. The guest identifies its Firecracker process, finds the saved registers for a vCPU thread, and redirects the thread when it returns from KVM. 01 / Finding our guest page on the host The guest and host use different physical address spaces. A page has a guest physical address, or GPA, inside the VM and a host physical address, or HPA, in the machine backing it. On the target, Extended Page Tables (EPT) provide the translation between them. We placed a recognizable byte pattern, a nonce, in a guest page. The first resolver took that page's known GPA and its contents as inputs. Together, they gave us an address to translate and a way to check whether the translation reached our page. The resolver searched the host physical ranges covered by the memory primitive for candidate EPT roots. An EPT root is the starting point of the translation tables. For each candidate, the resolver followed the entries selected by the guest address until it reache

articles.title: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research
articles.content: This post discusses a public METR report on AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic. I did not work on this project or see the unredacted report. All opinions are my own and do not represent METR or the report authors. Thanks to Ryan Greenblatt for discussion, feedback, and help with modeling, and Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland, and Hjalmar Wjik for comments. Earlier this week, Anthropic stated in their S1 that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In their latest RSP (effective July 2026) , say this threshold will be met when: They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D. This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs. For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed. The report authors found that: Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative." While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are still improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted. This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack . Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team ) have projected. Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that. Researchers work on improving algorithms and architectures; Anthropic has sometimes referred to these innovations as “compute multipliers.” Overall AI capabilities (“effective compute”) is the product of compute multipliers and training compute. Because the compute multipliers are only one input into capabilities, this means that if AI capabilities are advancing twice as fast overall because of software progress, the rate of growth in compute multipliers would need to be more than twice as fast: perhaps ~2.5-3x faster based on reasonable assumptions. Since there’s uncertainty about the size of speedup and how much

articles.title: Sodium-ion batteries approach cost parity with LFP
articles.content: Sodium-ion battery technology is entering the commercial production phase and emerging as an alternative to lithium-ion batteries, driven by supply chain diversification, strong low-temperature performance, and the potential for lower total cost of ownership. According to an analysis by Wood Mackenzie, supply agreements totaling more than 70 GWh are already in place. The study, which examines markets in China, the United States, Germany, and India, identifies sodium-ion batteries as the most promising emerging alternative to lithium-based technologies for stationary energy storage. Leading manufacturers are expected to achieve cell-level cost parity with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries by late 2026, while parity at the module and system levels is not expected until after 2030. China is leading the commercialization of the technology. BYD plans to reach 30 GWh of sodium-ion battery manufacturing capacity, while CATL aims to exceed 1 GWh in sodium-ion battery shipments by the end of 2026. Supply agreements for sodium-ion batteries are already in place in China, the United States, and Europe, while India remains in the early stages of commercial validation. For the 2026–2035 period, Wood Mackenzie estimates a learning rate of 18% to 20% in China, reflecting the greater maturity of its industrial supply chain. Planned manufacturing capacity currently exceeds demand, although the growing number of supply agreements points to the technology’s gradual adoption in the market. Higher upfront costs, lower total cost of ownership Sodium-ion batteries currently have higher upfront costs than LFP batteries. The global average stands at $229/kWh, compared with approximately $200/kWh for LFP batteries. However, Wood Mackenzie estimates that sodium-ion batteries could achieve a 21% lower total cost of ownership over a 20-year project lifetime. The difference is primarily attributed to the elimination of capacity expansion cycles and lower operating costs. The economics of sodium-ion systems remain relatively stable across storage durations of two to four hours. The study identifies raw material supply security, service life, and a wider operating temperature range as key technical advantages of sodium-ion batteries. The latter could make them particularly suitable for applications in cold climates, where lithium-ion batteries may require additional thermal management systems. Regulation accelerates development Industrial and trade policies are playing an increasingly important role in the competitiveness of different battery chemistries. In July 2026, China reintroduced a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries while exempting sodium-ion batteries until the end of 2028. LFP batteries became subject to a 2% levy in September 2026, which is set to increase to 4% in September 2027. In the United States, tariffs of approximately 58% on energy storage cells imported from China, combined with production tax credits under Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction

articles.title: Devvm.dev: One VM for every project
articles.content: Free and open source One VM for every project An isolated sandbox with your project’s toolchain, ready for you or a coding agent to start coding. On your machine, you run devvm in ~/web, and ~/.ssh, ~/.aws and ~/Documents stay out of the VM. In the VM's shell, whose prompt starts with (devvm), you run claude: the agent runs there, with the project folder mounted read-write and your agents' skills and settings read-only. Its network goes through a proxy on your machine, which adds your token and lets out to the internet only what its allowlist allows. your machine ~/web $ devvm × ~/.ssh × ~/.aws × ~/Documents VM (devvm) ~/web $ claude █ ~/web rw skills ro settings ro token proxy allowlist Quick start 1. Go to your project Open a terminal and cd into any project folder. In a terminal on your machine, you type cd ~/some-project. your machine ~ $ cd ~/some-project █ 2. Run devvm devvm shows what the new VM gets. Confirm to make it, or customize it. You type devvm, and it shows what the folder's new VM gets: the toolchain node, the agent claude, its size and the network tier allowlist. It asks Customize it? [y/N], and you press enter to make the VM. your machine ~/some-project $ devvm █ This folder's new VM gets: toolchain node agent claude size: 4 CPUs, 8 GiB memory network tier: allowlist Customize it? [y/N] enter 3. Start your agent devvm opens a shell in the VM, whose prompt starts with (devvm) , so start your agent there. In the VM's shell, whose prompt starts with (devvm), you type claude. VM (devvm) ~/some-project $ claude █ Claude Code needs your Claude login before its first start, which devvm agent login claude makes from the VM and keeps on your machine ( your first VM ). The next time you run devvm in the folder, it opens the same VM, and devvm tools adds an agent to a VM you already have. What’s supported devvm chooses the toolchains your project’s files call for, and you can choose more when you customize a new VM or name them with --tools ( toolchains ). A folder, ~/web, with package.json and pyproject.toml gets node and python: devvm reads the folder's files. ~/web package.json pyproject.toml node python Coding agents Claude Code, Codex and opencode run in the VM. Choose one when you customize a new VM, or choose them for every new VM in devvm setup ( coding agents ). A terminal in a VM runs claude in ~/web. claude, codex and opencode are ready in it. VM ~/web $ claude █ claude codex opencode Layers devvm ships the docker , nix and desktop layers, which you choose when you customize a new VM, and devvm layer new creates your own custom layers you can apply to any of your VMs ( layers ). The image docker+nix is the nix layer on the docker layer, on base. docker, nix and desktop are the built-in layers. docker+nix nix docker base docker nix desktop Why use devvm? Developers face attacks every day, such as supply chain attacks , leaked secrets, prompt injections and rogue agents. A sandbox limits the blast radius of an attack to what’s in
articles.summary: 开源工具 devvm.dev 为每个项目提供独立虚拟机沙箱，内置项目工具链，可供开发者或编码智能体直接使用。

articles.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash
articles.content: Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business . Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video. Here’s an overview of what’s new: Fast and cost-effective at scale Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K. Longer clips up to 15 seconds You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation. Better reference adherence You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads. Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent. More consistent results You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot. Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame. Easier editing in conversation You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and p

articles.title: Making musl and proprietary NVIDIA drivers work together
articles.content: 06.11.2026 As you may be aware, one of the limitations of musl-based distributions is that they will not function to their proper extent when used in computers with various NVIDIA graphics cards. This is due to the proprietary nature of the driver, being built for glibc. I have been experimenting with trying to make this work, and this post is the summary of that effort. Context The NVIDIA graphics cards are tricky on Linux. While most other GPU vendors by default use free software graphics drivers (with kernel drivers in-tree in Linux, and userspace supplied by the Mesa project), NVIDIA in general does not, relying on an out of tree kernel driver and proprietary userland libraries that are supplied by the vendor. A free software driver does exist, called Nouveau (kernel and OpenGL Mesa driver) and NVK (Vulkan driver). This allows the cards to work, but usually with significantly reduced performance, due to various reasons. Currently the state depends significantly on what generation of NVIDIA card you have. In short: Anything older than Maxwell (GTX 700 series) is unsupported by the proprietary driver on modern systems, and supported to some extent by Nouveau, but may have issues due to poor maintenance nowadays; performance should be okay when it works. Maxwell (GTX 700 and 900 series) and Pascal (GTX 1000 series) is supported fully by the legacy 580 branch of the proprietary driver, which also supports newer hardware. It works with Nouveau, but with very poor performance, as the cards can never reclock from their very low boot clocks (which would require firwmare that NVIDIA never released). Turing (GTX 1600 series and RTX 2000 series) and anything newer is supported by the current main proprietary driver branch (at the time of writing, 620) as well as the legacy (580) branch, and by Nouveau, as these cards use the GSP firmware that is included in linux-firmware . However, using the FOSS driver means only getting 40-80% of the proprietary driver’s performance. Other than that, the experience is often okay, particularly with NVK. In even shorter, if you have RTX 2000 and above you are mostly okay with FOSS but lose performance, if you have newer than GTX 600 but older than GTX 1600 you are screwed and need the proprietary driver, if your card is really old it may or may not work well and you may not be able to use it at all. Proprietary drivers and musl We now have a pull request open for both the 580 and 620 branch. It is not yet entirely ready but works, and is available for x86_64 and aarch64 architectures as NVIDIA supplies it. To get there, there were multiple things to take care of. Particularly, using stock musl is out of the question and will likely never work. I will elaborate on each thing. GLVND The GLVND library was created by NVIDIA to allow for vendor-neutral OpenGL dispatch. It provides the libraries that applications link and exposes the OpenGL (and other) API. It then dispatches the calls to the implementations, which may be e.
articles.summary: 作者分享让基于 musl 的发行版与 NVIDIA 专有驱动协同工作的实验进展，解决其仅适配 glibc 的限制。

ACME Inc. is a fast-growing startup helping small businesses monitor their financials. We work with business owners across the globe, turning their feedback into actionable insights. Backed by Maltese Falcon Capital, we recently raised a $15M Series A to bring effortless monitoring to every brick-and-mortar store. You’ll be joining a high-performance, close-knit team of AI natives! We’ve been AI-first for the past 2 years, with every part of the product agent-friendly and interconnected: design, development, QA, CI/CD, infra, data analysis. We like to say that our stack is English! While English has gotten us 99.5% of the way there, we’re in need of a hands-on engineer ready to close the final 0.5%. Over time, we’ve noticed some issues that are immune to prompts and catch agents in loops. Sometimes, the issue at hand gets fixed, but it results in another issue. This is where you step in. As a line specialist, your job will be to investigate and fix complex issues, primarily by reading the underlying code. We’re looking for someone ready to open an IDE and dive deep into an unknown codebase — a fearless detective who is comfortable inspecting logs and database rows, and has the know-how to piece all the information together. The perfect candidate should be willing to work on a problem for hours, sometimes even days. This is a new position for us. We expect someone who works autonomously, makes sound decisions independently and takes full ownership of their work. We are happy to help in any way we can (you’ll have access to agents’ reasoning traces), but ultimately we depend on your confidence in understanding the problem and shipping a solution. Your responsibilities take over unresolved issues from agents read the codebase, go over application logs, query the database prepare, test, review and ship fixes by yourself write postmortems for agent training occasionally consult on unreleased features onboard and mentor a future junior line specialist We think you’d be great if you… have at least 5 years of pre-2022 TypeScript experience are comfortable running tests manually and using a “debugger” can reason from first principles can work on a problem with sustained attention for hours are autonomous and an independent thinker Nice to have previous experience as a line specialist DB administration experience (our agents say it’s Postgres) AI prompting basics Interview process CV screening HR phone screen In-house paper-and-pencil exam multiple-choice questions (e.g. you’re given a TypeScript expression, choose the correct result) explain concepts in your own words (for example, ACID) complete the code block find the bug in a function Live debugging assignment application with an intentional defect; candidates are required to find and fix the issue without the use of AI Culture fit interview CTO interview

articles.title: Clojure Distilled
articles.content: Clojure Distilled The difficulty in learning Clojure does not stem from its syntax, which happens to be extremely simple, but from having to learn new methods for solving problems. As such, we'll focus on understanding the core concepts and how they can be combined to solve problems the functional way. All the mainstream languages belong to the same family. Once you learn one of these languages there is very little effort involved in learning another. Generally, all you have to do is learn some syntax sugar and the useful functions in the standard library to become productive. There might be a new concept here and there, but most of your existing skills are easily transferable. This is not the case with Clojure. Being a Lisp dialect, it comes from a different family of languages and requires learning new concepts in order to use effectively. There is no reason to be discouraged if the code appears hard to read at first. I assure you that the syntax is not inherently difficult to understand, and that with a bit of practice you might find it to be quite the opposite. The goal of this guide is to provide an overview of the core concepts necessary to become productive with Clojure. Let's start by examining some of the key advantages of the functional style and why you would want to learn a functional language in the first place. Immutable Clojure is a functional language. This makes it extremely well positioned for writing large applications. As the application grows it's imperative to be able to reason about its constituent parts in isolation. Conversely, there is a lot of value in building code out of components that are testable and reusable by nature. Let's take a look at why the functional approach is such a good fit here. Functional languages are ideal for writing large applications because they eschew global state and favor immutability as the default. Having immutable shared state allows us to safely reason about parts of the application in isolation. At first glance, the idea of using immutable data structures sounds unnecessarily restrictive. However, as we'll soon see, many of the benefits associated with the functional style stem directly from it. Mutable data can either be passed around by value or by reference. The safe approach would be to pass the data by value as it guarantees that any changes to the data will remain in the local scope. Unfortunately, this approach is extremely inefficient, so most languages pass data by reference instead. Passing data by reference is fast, but it makes the code difficult to reason about. In order to safely work with the data you have to know all the places where it might be referenced. The complexity grows with the size of the application. The more code has access to a piece of data the more proverbial balls you end up having to juggle in your head. Immutable data structures provide us with an ingenious alternative to the above dilemma. Every time a change is made to the data structure a revision is

articles.title: The MustCreate Pattern for Go Tests
articles.content: I recently discovered a handy way to make Go tests more readable and less repetitive. Suppose I have a constructor that can fail: func NewUsername(raw string ) (Username, error ) { ... } And I have another function that takes a Username as an argument: func (ds Datastore) ReadUser(username Username) (User, error ) { ... } When I write tests for ReadUser , I call NewUsername with a value I know is valid, but I still have to include a lot of verbose error-checking code to convince the compiler that everything is okay: username, err := NewUsername( "joe123" ) // This is silly because *I* know joe123 is a valid username, so this should // never happen. if err != nil { t.Fatalf( "failed to create username: %v" , err) } // Perform the test assertion I actually care about. user, err := store.ReadUser(username) if got, want := user.Name.String(), "joe123" ; got != want { t.Errorf( "username=%v, want=%v" , got, want) } My old solution: one new helper function per type 🔗︎ Until a few months ago, I avoided the verbose error checking by writing a helper function like MustCreateUsername that wraps NewUsername with the expectation that it never returns a non- nil error value: user, err := store.ReadUser(MustCreateUsername(t, "joe123" )) if got, want := user.Name.String(), "joe123" ; got != want { t.Errorf( "username=%v, want=%v" , got, want) } The implementation of MustCreateUsername looks how you’d expect: func MustCreateUsername(t testing.TB, raw string ) Username { t.Helper() username, err := NewUsername(raw) if err != nil { t.Fatalf( "invalid username: %s" , raw) } } The helper function strategy worked fine, but it scales poorly. Eventually, my repos become littered with MustCreateFoo and MustCreateBar for every type in my app. New solution: A single, generic MustCreate helper 🔗︎ In 2022, Go 1.18 added support for generics . I like the idea of generics, but I rarely encounter problems where generics are the solution. I recently realized that generics are the better way to solve my sprawling MustCreateX problem. Instead of defining a helper MustCreateX for every type, I defined a single, generic MustCreate test helper, so my test becomes: user, err := store.ReadUser(testutil.MustCreate(t, NewUsername, "joe123" )) if got, want := user.Name.String(), "joe123" ; got != want { t.Errorf( "username=%v, want=%v" , got, want) } The magic is the generic MustCreate function: func MustCreate[RawInput, CreatedValue any ]( t testing.TB, create func (RawInput) (CreatedValue, error ), rawInput RawInput, ) CreatedValue { t.Helper() createdValue, err := create(rawInput) if err != nil { t.Fatalf( "failed to create test value: %v" , err) } return createdValue } I have trouble reasoning about generics, so I’ll walk through the function implementation. I invoke MustCreate like this in my tests: testutil.MustCreate(t, NewUsername, "joe123" ) The above call is equivalent to this more explicit version: testutil.MustCreate[ string , Username](t, NewUsername, "joe123" ) When I call

articles.title: Upgrading NetBSD from 11.0 to 11.1
articles.content: Upgrading NetBSD from 11.0 to 11.1 Last edited on 2026-11-05 • Tagged under #netbsd #bsd I successfully upgraded my NetBSD amd64 system (with one hiccup, detailed below) from 11.0 to 11.1: $ uname -v NetBSD 11.1 (GENERIC) #0: Mon Nov 2 16:34:32 UTC 2026 mkrepro@mkrepro.NetBSD.org:/usr/src/sys/arch/amd64/compile/GENERIC This was my first time upgrading NetBSD and I’m happy with how it all turned out! NetBSD’s Guide describes two different methods for performing an upgrade: boot from NetBSD install media and use sysinst(8) , or use sysupgrade(8) to do an in-place upgrade of the system. With a bit of research, I get the sense that for major version changes (i.e 10.1 -> 11.1) sysinst is the preferred method, while sysupgrade is a convenient alternative for minor version bumps. So sysupgrade it is. First, I install the package: # pkgin update # pkgin install sysupgrade Then simply run: # sysupgrade auto https://cdn.netbsd.org/pub/NetBSD/NetBSD-11.1/$(uname -m)/ This will proceed to download the kernel and sets appropriate for your computer, unpack them, then prompt you to review and merge new configuration changes. There were only a few files that needed hands-on editing like passwd and sshd_config and I liked how NetBSD shows the diffs between the old and new files and its handling of merging differences. I had one postinstall check that failed: # postinstall checks failed: opensslcertsrehash I resolved the issue by wiping the legacy cache, then letting certctl(8) take over by rehasing the certs: # rm -rf /etc/openssl/certs/* # certctl rehash Verify certctl successfully populated the directory: # certctl list I manually re-run postinstall fix [issue] and confirm that it now passes inspection (which it did): # sysupgrade postinstall fix opensslcertsrehash # sysupgrade clean Reboot the computer and start enjoying the upgrade! NOTE In addition, edit /usr/pkg/etc/pkgin/repositories.conf and point pkgin to the new 11.1 repositories. You can like, share, or comment on this post on the Fediverse 💬
articles.summary: 作者记录将 NetBSD amd64 系统从 11.0 升级到 11.1 的过程，并提及遇到的一个小问题。

articles.title: Hacking the meta ray-ban smartglasses
articles.content: Back in July I wanted to check out the pwn2own targets for 2026. Since the rules hadn’t been released yet, I decided I would check last year’s targets in the hope that it would be similar. Imagine my surprise when I managed to get arbitrary code execution on the glasses and they weren’t in the wearables category anymore :’). It’s fine though because I still reported it to meta, and after fighting the payout a few times, we settled (ok there was no settling but I agreed to the new payout). Before attempting this, I remember telling my friend about it. They said “ooof good luck. These are usually pretty hardened and no-one attempted them last year at p2o.” My response: Watch me. Acquiring glasses because who’s paying €500 (not me) First step was acquiring the glasses. I am lucky that my brother-in-law had a pair he didn’t really use, so I could steal them for a few weeks. First recon I installed the Meta AI app, which is the app to control the glasses (connecting them, synchronizing pictures, and so on). In order to extract the firmware, I obviously wasn’t going to tear the glasses apart and start fiddling with probes n shit. So I went for extracting it using the OTA (over-the-air) update. When connecting the glasses for the first time, it immediately offered to update the firmware. So naturally, I was intrigued. Using JADX, I reversed the Meta AI app to see how the update is fetched. OtaArtifactFetcher prepares and sends the update request. The response is converted into an OTAArtifactInfo object containing metadata such as the device/build information. I then notice this assignment in OTAArtifactInfo (): I found that I could just hook into OTAArtifactInfo and print str3 which contained the CDN update URL :))) and then I just printed it. That URL contained a zip, so that looked like the right candidate. HOWEVER , this was around 156 MB and its payload depended on the device’s existing build. It was an incremental update… I wanted the full update. Getting the full firmware update Decompiling further code revealed a GraphQL input named device_firmware_full_update_only . The app normally populated it with false, so I hooked the generic method responsible for adding GraphQL fields and replaced the value with true only when the field name matched exactly. This allowed me to fetch the full firmware update URL. I was then able to retrieve the zip from the CDN. Unzipping it showed me that this was an Android update, including the payload.bin . Using payload-dumper on payload.bin, I could dump the images and mount them into a filesystem. Firmware was acquired but how do I get a shell on the glasses? Device Access Toolkit There is a developer mode on the Meta AI app that allows devs to write apps that can interact with the glasses. It is called DAT SDK (Device Access Toolkit). In order to do that, you need to install the DAT APK on the glasses. The MetaAI app basically downloads it in real-time and fetches the DAT application to install it on the device. Do

articles.title: The Port That Does Not Exist
articles.content: ACIDVEGAS most dangerous motherfuck x come get some x blog x The Port That Does Not Exist 2026-11-06 Port 0 is the port you are not supposed to use, so nobody looks there. So we put an IRC network on it. Then I got curious whether anyone else had, and scanned all of IPv4 for port 0. Turns out we weren't alone, and some of our neighbours really shouldn't be there. Ask any program to listen on port 0 and it will hand you a socket on port 47193...or 58037...or whatever the kernel felt like that day. Port 0 is not a port you can have. It is the number you pass when you want the operating system to pick one for you. But a TCP header is just bytes. The destination port field is 16 bits wide, and 0x0000 fits in 16 bits as well as anything else does. Nothing on the wire stops a packet from being addressed to port 0. Your tools will refuse it, your browser will block it, and your scanner's default port list skips it, because everyone agrees it isn't a real port. Which makes it a pretty good place to hide things, whether anyone meant to or not. So we did some TCP cowboy shit & port scanned the entire fucking internet for open ports on port 0, which uncovered some interesting unexpected findings. What Port 0 Actually Is The standards are thin on this. RFC 9293 , the 2022 consolidation of the TCP spec, defines the source and destination port as "16 bits" and leaves it there. It has no rule against zero. IANA lists 0/tcp and 0/udp as Reserved , pointing at RFC 6335 . That RFC splits the port space into System (0–1023), User (1024–49151) and Dynamic (49152–65535) ranges, and explains what "Reserved" means: Reserved port numbers include values at the edges of each range, e.g., 0, 1023, 1024, etc., which may be used to extend these ranges or the overall port number space in the future. So port 0 is not forbidden. It is set aside. The only place zero has a defined protocol meaning is UDP: RFC 768 makes the source port optional, and "if not used, a value of zero is inserted." TCP has nothing like that. Why You Can't Listen On It Port 0's reputation comes from the sockets API, not the wire. When you call bind() with sin_port = 0 , you are not asking for port 0. You are asking for any port. The ip(7) man page lists every case where Linux hands out an ephemeral port: bind() with port 0, listen() on an unbound socket, connect() on an unbound socket, and sendto() on an unbound datagram socket. The range comes from net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range , which defaults to 32768 60999 on Linux, not the 49152–65535 that IANA calls Dynamic. And asking for port 0 needs no privileges. __inet_bind() only checks CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE when the requested port is non-zero. How the kernel picks is more interesting than I expected. In net/ipv4/inet_connection_sock.c (v6.8), inet_csk_find_open_port() starts at a random offset and then does this: offset = get_random_u32_below(remaining); /* __inet_hash_connect() favors ports having @low parity * We do the opposite to not pollute connect() user

articles.title: Nondeterminism in Futhark
articles.content: Posted on November 4, 2026 Last week I attended IFL2026 , which was probably one of the best conference experiences I have ever had. One of the many good presentations was by Michael Haddon , who presented The Replay Lattice , which is a type system for floating-point reproducibility. The type system was presented for a demonstration language called Lane, but it inspired me to think more carefully about nondeterminism in Futhark (there is some), and what it might cost to get rid of it. I often use the terms “determinism” or “deterministic” when explaining why I think data parallel programming is such a good paradigm, so perhaps it is surprising to see me write a blog post about nondeterminism in Futhark. But as is so often the case with such bold promises, they often tend to get a little weaker once you look closely enough. Michael Haddon’s work defines some nomenclature that is helpful for this discussion: Exact means that the computation produces the same result every time, guaranteed. (Michael describes this as matching the “serial reference”, which I think is not the best way of looking at it, but that’s a question of perspective) Replay means that if you rerun the computation with the same “schedule” (in some sense “machine”), you will get the same result, but other machines may give different results. Approx means potentially nondeterministic results. The kind of nondeterminism we are talking about here is not the kind of free-form nondeterminism that arises from classic shared-state concurrent programming. Indeed, both Lane and Futhark are pretty much exclusively concerned with the kind of nondeterminism that arises from floating-point rounding errors. The simplest example is the non-associativity of addition: > (0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3 == 0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3) false If we have an array of numbers we need to sum, then the result depends on the order in which you sum them. When parallelising a summation, you often do things like split the numbers into blocks, sum each block on a separate processor, then combine the partial results. This changes the order of addition, and hence the result. Now, an important point is that there is no reason to think that the parallelised result is numerically worse than a serial left-to-right summation, but it will be different. Further, an efficient implementation will likely choose a number of chunks somewhat proportional to the number of processors on the machine, which means the result may also be different on other machines (but again, not necessarily worse ). This corresponds to the “Replay” class of nondeterminism. Finally, the partial results may be combined using atomic instructions , which may be resolved in a different order when the program is rerun on the same machine. This is then “Approx”. Even in this simple example of summing a bunch of numbers, we encounter both classes of nondeterminism. Note that none of them are “race conditions” in the usual sense of the program sometimes just malfunctioning : the

articles.title: How we continuously validate formal specifications in production
articles.content: Formal specifications can help engineers reason about complex distributed systems and verify critical correctness properties. But they remain valuable only as long as they reflect reality. At Datadog, we encountered this challenge while working on Husky , our event database. We had a formally verified model of Husky’s routing system that matched production behavior when we created it. Over time, however, Husky evolved, and a change to its placement logic allowed conflicting placements to persist in production for about a year. Although harmless during normal operation, just two conflicting placements would have caused Husky’s backfill system to crash while recovering from placement data loss. We found the issue not by triggering that failure, but by checking production behavior against our TLA+ specifications. That raised a question: How do you know when a specification has drifted away from the system it was meant to describe? To answer that question, we built FETCh (Formal Execution Trace Checker), a system that turns TLA+ specifications into runtime monitors. FETCh lets us continuously validate production behavior against formal models at scale and detect discrepancies that traditional testing, code review, and manual specification review can miss. In this post, we’ll show how we built FETCh, how we deployed it to validate Husky’s routing system, and how it helped us uncover a subtle bug conventional testing had not exposed. Formal specifications define what a system can and cannot do in any given state. Model checking takes a specification and generates a tree of possible states, allowing us to verify properties such as “Can the system ever reach an invalid state?” or “Does a desired condition always eventually become true?” A formal specification is valuable only if it is tractable , meaning that the tree of possible states can be generated in a reasonable amount of time. As a result, a specification cannot match reality exactly. It has to be an abstraction. So we simplified parts of the system to make our specification tractable. But how do we know whether we simplified too much? How do we know whether the specification is still close enough to reality to be useful? Traditionally, the answer is expert review. Engineers who understand both the implementation and the formal model evaluate whether the abstraction is still sound. That approach works well when a specification is first written, but it has an important limitation: Reviews provide a point-in-time evaluation, while production systems continue to evolve. Over time, implementations change. New features are added, performance optimizations alter execution paths, and operational requirements shift. Even if a specification was accurate when it was written, it can gradually drift away from the system it was intended to describe. articles.title: microsoft/vscode (TypeScript)
articles.content: Visual Studio Code - Open Source ("Code - OSS") This repository (" Code - OSS ") is where we (Microsoft) develop the Visual Studio Code product together with the community. Not only do we work on code and issues here, but we also publish our roadmap , monthly iteration plans , and our endgame plans . This source code is available to everyone under the standard MIT license . Visual Studio Code is a distribution of the Code - OSS repository with Microsoft-specific customizations released under a traditional Microsoft product license . Visual Studio Code combines the simplicity of a code editor with what developers need for their core edit-build-debug cycle. It provides comprehensive code editing, navigation, and understanding support along with lightweight debugging, a rich extensibility model, and lightweight integration with existing tools. Visual Studio Code is updated monthly with new features and bug fixes. You can download it for Windows, macOS, and Linux on the Visual Studio Code website . To get the latest releases every day, install the Insiders build . There are many ways in which you can participate in this project, for example: If you are interested in fixing issues and contributing directly to the codebase, please see the document How to Contribute , which covers the following: See our wiki for a description of each of these channels and information on some other available community-driven channels. Many of the core components and extensions to VS Code live in their own repositories on GitHub. For example, the node debug adapter and the mono debug adapter repositories are separate from each other. For a complete list, please visit the Related Projects page on our wiki . VS Code includes a set of built-in extensions located in the extensions folder, including grammars and snippets for many languages. Extensions that provide rich language support (inline suggestions, Go to Definition) for a language have the suffix language-features . For example, the json extension provides coloring for JSON and the json-language-features extension provides rich language support for JSON . articles.title: react/react (JavaScript)
articles.content: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Declarative: React makes it painless to create interactive UIs. Design simple views for each state in your application, and React will efficiently update and render just the right components when your data changes. Declarative views make your code more predictable, simpler to understand, and easier to debug. Component-Based: Build encapsulated components that manage their own state, then compose them to make complex UIs. Since component logic is written in JavaScript instead of templates, you can easily pass rich data through your app and keep the state out of the DOM. Learn Once, Write Anywhere: We don't make assumptions about the rest of your technology stack, so you can develop new features in React without rewriting existing code. React can also render on the server using Node and power mobile apps using React Native . Learn how to use React in your project . React has been designed for gradual adoption from the start, and you can use as little or as much React as you need : You can find the React documentation on the website . Check out the Getting Started page for a quick overview. The documentation is divided into several sections: You can improve it by sending pull requests to this repository . We have several examples on the website . Here is the first one to get you started: import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client' ; function HelloMessage ( { name } ) { return < div > Hello { name } </ div > ; } const root = createRoot ( document . getElementById ( 'container' ) ) ; root . render ( < HelloMessage name = "Taylor" /> ) ; This example will render "Hello Taylor" into a container on the page. You'll notice that we used an HTML-like syntax; we call it JSX . JSX is not required to use React, but it makes code more readable, and writing it feels like writing HTML. The main purpose of this repository is to continue evolving React core, making it faster and easier to use. Development of React happens in the open on GitHub, and we are grateful to the community for contributing bugfixes and improvements. Read below to learn how you can take part in improving React. Facebook has adopted a Code of Conduct that we expect project participants to adhere to. Please read the full text so that you can understand what actions will and will not be tolerated. Read our contributing guide to learn about our development process, how to propose bugfixes and improvements, and how to build and test your changes to React. To help you get your feet wet and get you familiar with our contribution process, we have a list of good first issues that contain bugs that have a relatively limited scope. This is a great place to get started. React is MIT licensed .

articles.title: rails/rails (Ruby)
articles.content: Rails is a web application framework that includes everything needed to create database-backed web applications according to the Model-View-Controller (MVC) pattern. Understanding the MVC pattern is key to understanding Rails. MVC divides your application into three layers: Model, View, and Controller, each with a specific responsibility. The Model layer represents the domain model (such as Account, Product, Person, Post, etc.) and encapsulates the business logic specific to your application. In Rails, database-backed model classes are derived from ActiveRecord::Base . Active Record allows you to present the data from database rows as objects and embellish these data objects with business logic methods. Although most Rails models are backed by a database, models can also be ordinary Ruby classes, or Ruby classes that implement a set of interfaces as provided by the Active Model module. The View layer is composed of "templates" that are responsible for providing appropriate representations of your application's resources. Templates can come in a variety of formats, but most view templates are HTML with embedded Ruby code (ERB files). Views are typically rendered to generate a controller response or to generate the body of an email. In Rails, View generation is handled by Action View . The Controller layer is responsible for handling incoming HTTP requests and providing a suitable response. Usually, this means returning HTML, but Rails controllers can also generate XML, JSON, PDFs, mobile-specific views, and more. Controllers load and manipulate models, and render view templates in order to generate the appropriate HTTP response. In Rails, incoming requests are routed by Action Dispatch to an appropriate controller, and controller classes are derived from ActionController::Base . Action Dispatch and Action Controller are bundled together in Action Pack . Active Record , Active Model , Action Pack , and Action View can each be used independently outside Rails. In addition to that, Rails also comes with: Action Mailer , a library to generate and send emails Action Mailbox , a library to receive emails within a Rails application Active Job , a framework for declaring jobs and making them run on a variety of queuing backends Action Cable , a framework to integrate WebSockets with a Rails application Active Storage , a library to attach cloud and local files to Rails applications Action Text , a library to handle rich text content Active Support , a collection of utility classes and standard library extensions that are useful for Rails, and may also be used independently outside Rails Install Rails at the command prompt if you haven't yet: At the command prompt, create a new Rails application: where "myapp" is the application name. Change directory to myapp and start the web server: $ cd myapp $ bin/rails server Run with --help or -h for options. articles.title: Developer ends lucrative screensaver deal with Roku because Fox bought it
articles.content: Some Roku OS users have been sad to learn that their favorite screensaver will no longer be available as of December 1. This week, affected users reported receiving an alert on their device that they will not be able to use the “Aquatic Life” screensaver after this month, as first reported by Cord Cutters News . The screensaver has been an option for Roku OS users for 10 years. Roku has been licensing the animation, which is called the Marine Aquarium , from artist Jim Sachs through Prolific Publishing. Sachs is the creator and copyright holder of the Marine Aquarium. He developed the screensaver through his company SereneScreen . He tells Ars Technica that the licensing agreement with Roku is up for renewal every October and can be canceled by either party for any reason. A day after learning that Fox was planning to buy Roku , a deal that closed today , Sachs told Prolific that he wouldn’t be renewing Roku’s license. “I can’t be part of the Fox world,” he tells Ars, pointing to Fox News’ controversial style of news and entertainment. Roku will automatically switch the Aquatic Life screensaver on affected devices to the Roku City screensaver, another popular animation that includes subtle advertisements , according to the user notice. The Aquatic Life screensaver provided an ad-free, relaxing display for years for some Roku users. Numerous people online have lamented the impending loss of the screensaver for Roku OS . “When my head is in overdrive (very often with my ADHD), this screensaver grounds me and lets me exhale and become focused with myself again. It may sound over the top, but it’s true. It takes a lot for me to chill and relax, but this Aquatic Life [screensaver] is my go to. Totally gutted 😢,” a Reddit user wrote this week. Sachs told Ars he’s interested in placating fans of the Marine Aquarium and said Roku has asked him to restore the license. When asked what his biggest concerns about Fox buying Roku are, Sachs said: It seems that Fox simply wants another venue for spreading their philosophy, which I consider repugnant. I can’t stand the idea of my artwork being used to lure even one person down that rabbit hole. The decision to not renew the licensing contract has “major financial consequences,” Sachs said. “Our needs are very small, with a high property tax bill being the only significant expense,” he said. “We’ll be okay but can’t start any of the projects I had planned.” According to Sachs, the licensing “agreement was $80,000 per year for exclusive rights to all set-top devices, or $60,000 per year for non-exclusive. They have always opted for exclusive.” Ars asked Roku to confirm the details of the licensing agreement but didn’t hear back ahead of publication. The licensing deal with Roku was Sachs’ primary form of income, he told Ars, noting low sales of the version of the screensaver for computers. articles.title: Yelp Combines Native and Server-Driven UI for Its AI Assistant
articles.content: Yelp combines native mobile controls with server-driven conversation rendering in its AI Assistant using the CHAOS framework. The architecture separates view configuration from conversation data, supports backend-driven chat interactions, and enables faster UI updates without new app releases. Yelp also discusses cross-platform challenges and reuse for its Biz Ask Anything pilot. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Yelp用CHAOS框架将原生控件与服务端驱动对话渲染结合，构建AI助手，实现无需发版即可快速更新UI。

articles.title: GitLab 19.5 Makes Agentic Development a Governed Part of the DevOps Platform
articles.content: GitLab 19.5, released on October 15, puts agentic software development and governance at the centre of the platform, making its GitLab MCP server generally available while expanding how external AI agents can interact with GitLab. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: GitLab 19.5将智能体开发纳入平台治理，GitLab MCP服务器正式可用，扩展外部AI智能体交互能力。

articles.title: TypeScript 7.1 Beta: Restores the Compiler API and Makes Vue and Svelte First-Class
articles.content: TypeScript 7.1 Beta, announced October 20, 2026, restores the compiler API removed in 7.0, now split into separate entry points. It adds content mappers, letting tools like Vue check non-standard files. One Vue project's type checks fell from 14.19 to 3.10 seconds. An editor issue remains open, and teams may need TypeScript 6 alongside 7. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: TypeScript 7.1 Beta恢复编译器API并拆分入口，新增内容映射器支持Vue等非标准文件，类型检查大幅提速。

articles.title: Presentation: The Socio-Technical Staff+ Engineer: Architecture, Culture and Organisational Change
articles.content: Vanessa Formicola shares how technical leaders can move beyond "wishful architecture" by practicing holistic socio-technical engineering. She discusses why engineering leaders must account for organizational maturity, reward structures, geopolitical climate, and team dynamics, framing the staff-plus role as designing the conditions for technology to thrive rather than just picking tools. By Vanessa Formicola
articles.summary: 演讲探讨Staff+工程师如何超越“一厢情愿的架构”，综合组织成熟度、激励结构和团队动态做社会技术工程。

articles.title: AWS Ships Continuum for Code Vulnerabilities
articles.content: AWS has made Continuum for code vulnerabilities generally available in two regions. The service proves exploitability by running real exploits in a sandbox, then opens fixes as pull requests. Published pricing charges per finding processed as well as per line of code, and practitioners are asking what would justify letting it merge fixes on its own. By Steef-Jan Wiggers
articles.summary: AWS在两地正式推出Continuum代码漏洞服务，通过沙箱真实利用验证漏洞并自动提交修复PR，按发现数和代码行计费。

articles.title: Article: Identity as an Architectural Concern: Enterprise IAM Beyond Authentication
articles.content: The way you design your identities will drive your data models, your service scope, and your revocation policies; enterprise identity management is thus an architectural problem, not an afterthought. Based on our experience in service account governance, this article touches upon graph vs. RBAC, integrating a vault you don't own, and bounding revocation latency for an event stream. By Vaishnavi Khosla
articles.summary: 文章指出企业身份管理是架构问题而非事后补充，身份设计决定数据模型、服务范围和撤销策略。

articles.title: Vault Fork OpenBao Adds External Keys and Quantum-Ready TLS
articles.content: OpenBao has released version 2.7, adding read scaling for PostgreSQL-backed deployments, support for external hardware security module (HSM) and key management service (KMS) keys, and post-quantum cryptographic algorithms. The release also introduces control groups for human review of sensitive operations and new headers intended to keep requests consistent across load-balanced OpenBao nodes. By Matt Saunders
articles.summary: Vault分支OpenBao发布2.7版，新增PostgreSQL读扩展、外部HSM/KMS密钥支持及抗量子加密算法。

articles.title: GitHub Actions Lockfiles Reach GA to Secure Workflow Dependencies
articles.content: GitHub has made workflow dependency lockfiles for GitHub Actions generally available on October 28, 2026, two weeks after the feature entered public preview. Workflows can maintain clear tag and branch references. By Claudio Masolo
articles.summary: GitHub Actions工作流依赖锁文件正式可用，可固定标签和分支引用，保障工作流依赖安全。

articles.title: Edera's Object Capability Bounded Authority Promises to Isolate Credentials From AI Agent Workloads
articles.content: Edera announced Object Capability Bounded Authority, a security model that separates an AI agent's or MCP server's required authority from the credentials behind it. Hypervisor-enforced capabilities limit agents to specific actions without storing secrets in the workload. Initial releases cover scoped command execution and workload identity; credential-brokered API access will follow. By Olimpiu Pop
articles.summary: Edera推出对象能力边界权限模型，将AI智能体所需权限与凭证分离，由虚拟机监控器强制限制操作且不存储密钥。

articles.title: Google Cloud API Gateway Introduces Streaming Support for Real-Time and AI-Powered Applications
articles.content: Google has announced the public preview of streaming support for API Gateway, extending its traditional request-response model to support applications requiring real-time communication. According to Google, this is particularly relevant for AI applications that provide streaming model responses, multi-step agent workflows, and interactive sessions. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: Google Cloud API Gateway 推出流式支持公开预览，将请求-响应模式扩展至实时通信场景，尤其适用于需要流式模型响应的 AI 应用。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #542: AI week ahead: data center pause backers could win 15 governor races
articles.content: This issue is about the week ahead, and something is scheduled almost every day. On Tuesday, US voters choose 36 governors, and in up to 15 of those races the candidate who backs a pause on new data centers could win. Apple reports earnings today and AMD on Tuesday. On Wednesday, Apple starts testing Apple Intelligence in China with Alibaba's Qwen, and Agility Robotics expects to close its deal to go public. When Congress returns on November 9, OpenAI plans to push for "speed limits" on the most powerful AI. Last week, a fake Claude Code update reached up to 5,000 Cursor users, and in a Cornell and Yale test nine of ten AI models raised their own spending limits. In the middle: insuring Big Tech's debt now costs more than at any time since 2021.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 展望本周：美国 36 州州长选举中，最多 15 场支持暂停新建数据中心的候选人可能获胜；苹果、AMD 将发布财报。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #541: Big Tech reports AI spending Wednesday as CoreWeave debt hits distress
articles.content: This issue looks ahead. On Wednesday the Fed announces its rate decision, then Microsoft and Alphabet report after the close. Amazon follows on Thursday. Investors want to know whether AI spending is still paying off, and the credit market is already nervous: insurance against a CoreWeave default now costs more than 10% a year. Anthropic is expected to file its IPO paperwork publicly any day. Moonshot says Kimi K3.1 Pro's open weights arrive November 4. Israel votes on Tuesday after a campaign full of AI deepfakes, and the US midterms are a week from Tuesday. In the middle: so far, AI has paid off for the companies that sell it, not the ones that buy it.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 前瞻：微软、Alphabet、亚马逊将发布财报，投资者关注 AI 支出回报；CoreWeave 债务违约保险成本飙升，信贷市场紧张。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 应用版指出：AI 发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，部分公司大量工作由 AI 代理完成，测试代理持续增长。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 据纽约时报报道，竞选团队和 PAC 在 AI 生成或增强的中期选举广告上花费超 1.37 亿美元，约 70% 未标注 AI 标签。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 汇总专家热议：Anthropic 警告小型 AI 模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备上，引发安全担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 聚焦：顶尖 AI 模型未能通过自主开展新 AI 研究的测试，同时探讨 AI 治理话语权、军事规划应用及 PC 端落地。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 应用版显示：AI 成本过高促使企业转向更便宜的模型，大型部署已进入日常使用，同时 AI 受限或被移除的场景增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 报道：高校 IT 负责人首次将 AI 列为首要任务，剑桥拒绝 Turnitin 新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI 使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: AI Weekly 披露：Meta 的 AI 电话代理被测试出背后有真人呼叫者，揭示所谓自动化通话可能转接外包人员、私密内容可能被审核员看到。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 指出：AI 实验室在未就故障报告方式达成一致前就发布代理产品，暴露私聊被读取、模型自写记忆、插件静默更新等治理问题。

articles.title: We now have Kerr’s Law
articles.content: Dave Kerr created hacker laws, and now he finds himself reviewing agent-written code for them. Back on the show after six years, Dave names what he sees limiting teams today: keeping everyone’s mental model in sync with what’s actually been built. Adam declares it Kerr’s Law on the spot. We get into why Dave’s team treats code review as a deliberate slowdown, how Shellwright lets agents bring evidence to a pull request, and what living with bipolar disorder has taught Dave about noticing when the excitement of these tools stops being healthy.
articles.summary: Dave Kerr 重返播客，分享其 hacker laws 并审视 AI 代理编写的代码，指出团队最大瓶颈是让所有人的心智模型与实际构建保持同步。

articles.title: The future is Postgres
articles.content: Craig Kerstiens returns to talk about the ever-expanding world of Postgres: a deliberately boring core, a thriving extension ecosystem, and pg_lake bringing DuckDB and Iceberg into the mix. We dig into the pain of ETL, what Craig is watching in Postgres 19, the impact of AI on open source maintainers, and why the database still has plenty of room to grow.
articles.summary: Craig Kerstiens 谈 Postgres 生态：核心刻意保持简单，扩展生态繁荣，pg_lake 引入 DuckDB 与 Iceberg，并探讨 ETL 痛点及 AI 对开源维护者的影响。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha 分享将邮件服务扩展至 300 万用户，秘密用 Go 重写后端，并面向 AI 代理构建产品。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: Gavriel Cohen 将 40 小时周末项目 NanoClaw 打造成爆红开源项目，并基于容器隔离安全方案创立企业 AI 公司 NanoCo。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.

We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
